Refuse a fit that this session's memory cap cannot hold

Source: R/fit-memory.R
guard_memory.Rd

Call this at the top of a fit chunk, with the memory the fit is expected to need. It reads the memory limit of the session (the Linux cgroup, falling back to the machine's physical memory) and stops, in the first minutes of a render, when the need exceeds 90 percent of it. The refusal names the Workbench profile that would hold the fit and, when cores_fit is given, the largest cores that would fit in this session.

Usage

guard_memory(
  need_gib,
  why,
  cores = NULL,
  cores_fit = NULL,
  proc = "/proc/self/cgroup",
  sys = "/sys/fs/cgroup"
)

Arguments

need_gib

Expected peak memory of the fit, in GiB. 0 (a cached re-render) and NA (no estimate) pass.

why

Character(1). What needs the memory, in a few words, for the message, best with the counts the estimate was made from ("this boostmtree fit (1,391 patients, 4,771 visits, continuous)").

cores

Number of parallel workers the fit would use, a whole number of at least 1, or NULL.

cores_fit

A function taking a number of cores and returning the GiB the fit would need, or NULL. Used only to name a core count that fits.

proc, sys

Paths of the cgroup files, for tests. The defaults read the running session.

Value

The session's memory limit in GiB, invisibly, when the fit fits. Otherwise an error whose text begins memory:.

Details

A detached job counts against its submitting session's cgroup, so this is the cap the fit will hit. On cgroup v1 the recorded peak is the session's, not the job's alone. Workbench enforces about 1.2 times the memory its profile advertises, and the profile caps used here are those enforced values.

Examples

# \donttest{
# Without a cgroup (macOS, Windows) this falls back to the machine's physical memory.
guard_memory(1, "a small fit")
# }
